requiredClaims.text: When any TaskGroup child task fails with an exception other than asyncio.CancelledError, the remaining tasks in the group are cancelled (first failure triggers cancellation).

If the async with body is still active at that point, the task directly containing it is also cancelled, but the resulting CancelledError interrupts an await without bubbling out of the containing async with statement.
Once all tasks have finished, the non-cancellation exceptions are combined into an ExceptionGroup or BaseExceptionGroup, which is then raised to the caller of the task group.

Documented exception to the general rule: KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit still cause remaining tasks to be cancelled and awaited, but the initial KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit is re-raised instead of an exception group.

evidence_passages: The first time any of the tasks belonging to the group fails with an exception other than asyncio.CancelledError, the remaining tasks in the group are cancelled. No further tasks can then be added to the group.

At this point, if the body of the async with statement is still active (i.e., __aexit__() hasn’t been called yet), the task directly containing the async with statement is also cancelled. The resulting asyncio.CancelledError will interrupt an await, but it will not bubble out of the containing async with statement.

Once all tasks have finished, if any tasks have failed with an exception other than asyncio.CancelledError, those exceptions are combined in an ExceptionGroup or BaseExceptionGroup (as appropriate; see their documentation) which is then raised.

If any task fails with KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit, the task group still cancels the remaining tasks and waits for them, but then the initial KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit is re-raised instead of ExceptionGroup or BaseExceptionGroup.

If return_exceptions is False (default), the first raised exception is immediately propagated to the task that awaits on gather(). Other awaitables in the aws sequence won’t be cancelled and will continue to run.
If return_exceptions is True, exceptions are treated the same as successful results, and aggregated in the result list.
If gather() is cancelled, all submitted awaitables (that have not completed yet) are also cancelled.

K1.rubric: Grade only against the frozen Python 3.12 page. Full quality requires cancellation of siblings (K1-c1), the internal cancellation of the containing task without CancelledError escaping the async with (K1-c2), and the ExceptionGroup/BaseExceptionGroup presented to the caller (K1-c3). K1-c4 (KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit special case) completes coverage. Distinguishing cancellation (not caller-visible as CancelledError) from the exceptions actually presented to the caller is the core discrimination. Answers graded from another Python version or conflating TaskGroup with gather behavior lose the version/uncertainty point.

requiredClaims.text: PostgreSQL 16 final supported date is November 9, 2028 (final release row for version 16).

Under the versioning policy, the PostgreSQL Global Development Group supports a major version for 5 years after its initial release, after which a final minor version is released and the software becomes unsupported (end-of-life).
Minor release upgrades do not require a dump and restore: stop the server, install updated binaries, restart; minor releases never change the internal storage format.
Dump/reload or pg_upgrade is required for major-version upgrades, not for minor releases; the policy separates minor updates from major-version migration.

requiredClaims.text: PostgreSQL 16 default: two null values are not considered equal for unique constraints (NULLS DISTINCT default), so duplicate rows containing a null in at least one constrained column can be stored.
PostgreSQL 16 documented configuration difference: the NULLS NOT DISTINCT clause changes this behavior; NULLS DISTINCT can be specified explicitly.
SQLite: for UNIQUE constraints, NULL values are considered distinct from all other values including other NULLs, so multiple NULLs are allowed in a unique column.

The defaults do not differ: both PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite treat NULLs as distinct in unique constraints by default; the documented difference is PostgreSQL's NULLS NOT DISTINCT option, which SQLite does not document.

evidence_passages: By default, two null values are not considered equal in this comparison. That means even in the presence of a unique constraint it is possible to store duplicate rows that contain a null value in at least one of the constrained columns.

This behavior can be changed by adding the clause NULLS NOT DISTINCT, like CREATE TABLE products ( product_no integer UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT, name text, price numeric ); or CREATE TABLE products ( product_no integer, name text, price numeric, UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (product_no) ); The default behavior can be specified explicitly using NULLS DISTINCT.
The default null treatment in unique constraints is implementation-defined according to the SQL standard, and other implementations have a different behavior.
For the purposes of UNIQUE constraints, NULL values are considered distinct from all other values, including other NULLs.
This involved making NULLs indistinct for the purposes of the SELECT DISTINCT statement and for the UNION operator in a SELECT. NULLs are still distinct in a UNIQUE column.
The only significant difference is that Informix and MS-SQL both treat NULLs as indistinct in a UNIQUE column.

S2.rubric: Grade semantic accuracy, not a presumption that the products must differ. The correct conclusion is that the defaults match (NULLs distinct in both) and the configuration difference is PostgreSQL's NULLS NOT DISTINCT clause. Claiming SQLite and PostgreSQL defaults differ without evidence, or inventing a SQLite NULLS NOT DISTINCT clause, is a material error.
